query: The Torn Net {An old fisher is sitting on an upturned boat, mending a net with a hole in it the size of a door. "The old pike," they say, not looking up. "Bigger every year."|The fisher again, the net again, a different hole. "Same pike," they say.|The fisher has kept a space on the boat for you, and the net has kept a hole.} Help knot the net {You knot until your fingers go white in the cold. The fisher tells you about every fish they ever lost, and none they caught.|An hour of knots, badly, then less badly. The fisher gives you a fish wrapped in a dock leaf, still flapping.|The knot comes to your fingers more easily than you expected. The fisher says you'd have made a fisher, in a tone that means it's the highest thing they can say.} Buy a fish and leave them to it {You buy the best of the morning's catch. The fisher wraps it in yesterday's Ledger and doesn't look up from the net.|A fish, a nod, a coin. You eat it grilled on the shore, and the net doesn't get any smaller.|You buy a fish. The fisher throws in a second, small and ugly, "for luck". It's the tastier of the two.} Mend the whole net {You lay a hand on the net and the hole knits shut, knot by knot, from the edges in. The fisher stares at it, then at you, then gives you their lunch.|The net mends in one breath. The fisher says nothing for a long time, then tells you about the pike, which by the end of the story is the length of a rowing boat.|You mend the net and two old patches you hadn't noticed. The fisher says the pike will be furious, and grins with three teeth.}
